approachQuestion.prompt: A rectangular floor plan is an r by c binary grid, with 1 ≤ r,c and r×c ≤ 200,000. Return the greatest number of cells in an axis-aligned rectangle consisting entirely of 1s, or 0 if none exists. Example: [[1,0,1],[1,1,1]] returns 3 from the bottom row. Choose the best approach.
constraints: The immutable binary grid has r rows and c columns, with 1 ≤ r,c and r×c ≤ 200,000. Counts and areas fit machine words; array access and arithmetic have unit cost.
Input and returned output are excluded from auxiliary space. Working stacks, arrays, and copies count. No hashing is used.

options.text: Maintain c column heights of consecutive 1s ending at the current row. For each row, find its largest histogram rectangle with an increasing index stack, evaluating popped heights using the current index and new top as boundaries; flush at row end. Keep the greatest area.
options.feedback: Every all-1 rectangle has a bottom row. In that row its column heights support its full height, so the histogram calculation considers an area at least as large; every histogram rectangle also represents actual 1 cells.

options.text: Return the longest consecutive run of 1s in any single row.
options.feedback: A rectangle may span rows. For [[1,1],[1,1]], the answer is 4 rather than 2.

options.text: For each row sum all its column heights and return the maximum sum.
options.feedback: Different heights do not form a single rectangle. For [[1,0],[1,1]], the bottom heights [2,1] sum to 3, but the largest rectangle has area 2.

options.text: Enumerate all top, bottom, left, and right boundaries and inspect every cell inside each candidate.
options.feedback: It tests the definition correctly but repeats overlapping cell inspections across a vast number of rectangles. The row-height method avoids that enumeration.

feedback.reason: Reduce a two-dimensional rectangle search to one-dimensional height boundaries for each bottom row.
details: Update consecutive-one heights for each new row, resetting a column to zero at a 0. Run the increasing-height index-stack rectangle calculation on this row, then clear the stack before processing the next row. Equal heights may remain; the leftmost equal candidate eventually captures their full width.

For each bottom row, heights count consecutive ones ending there. A histogram rectangle corresponds exactly to an all-one grid rectangle with that bottom. Reset zero cells and reuse the stack between rows.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For row-height-rectangles, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n=r×c denote the number of cells. Allocate a height array and a reused stack of c indices; no transformed grid is stored.
constraints: Stack push, pop, and top take amortized constant time using a growable array; each entry uses a constant number of words. Count the working stack, but exclude input and final output. No recursive call stack or hash table is used.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(c) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each row has linear stack work; only column-height state survives between rows.
details: Each cell updates one height. Within each row every index is pushed once and popped at most once, so total time is O(r×c)=O(n). The height array and reused stack occupy O(c) auxiliary space.
